hints: Think about why $\text{AlCl}_3$ dimerises at lower temperature. Count electrons around Al in the monomer to see why it wants two more bonds.
Recall what a coordinate bond means for arrow direction, and consider which $\text{Cl}$ atoms can donate a lone pair to bridge the two Al centres.
walkthrough:
See why the monomer is hungry**
In $\text{AlCl}_3$, Al has only 6 electrons in its outer shell, it is electron deficient. At $200^{\circ}\text{C}$ two molecules join together so each Al can reach an octet by accepting lone pairs from Cl on the other molecule.

Build the bridged dimer**
Picture two $\text{AlCl}_3$ units side by side. Two Cl atoms sit in the middle as bridges, each bonded to both Al atoms, while each Al keeps two terminal Cl atoms outside. That gives formula $\text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$.

Mark the dative bonds**
A bridging Cl already has a normal covalent bond to one Al, then it donates a lone pair into the empty orbital of the second Al. Show this second bond as an arrow pointing from Cl to Al. You need two such arrows, one from each bridging Cl, to earn full credit.

Final answer: Dimer $\text{Cl}_2\text{Al}(\mu\text{-Cl})_2\text{AlCl}_2$ with two bridging Cl atoms linking the two Al atoms. Each Al bonded to two terminal Cl by normal covalent bonds and to two bridging Cl, with two $\text{Cl} \rightarrow \text{Al}$ coordinate bonds clearly shown as arrows.

hints: Count bonding pairs and lone pairs on Al in gaseous $\text{AlCl}_3$ to work out its shape.
walkthrough:
Read the shape from electron pairs**
In $\text{AlCl}_3(\text{g})$, Al has three bonding pairs and no lone pairs. Three regions repel equally to give a trigonal planar shape, so the $\text{Cl-Al-Cl}$ angle is $120^{\circ}$.

hints: Write the atomic configurations of Li (3 electrons) and H (1 electron), then adjust for loss and gain of one electron.
walkthrough:
Add and remove one electron**
Li is $1s^22s^1$, losing the $2s$ electron leaves $\text{Li}^+$ as $1s^2$. H is $1s^1$, gaining one electron gives $\text{H}^-$ as $1s^2$. Both end up with the stable helium configuration.
Final answer: $\text{Li}^+$ is $1s^2$ and $\text{H}^-$ is $1s^2$

hints: Picture what particles are present in an alloy of two metals and what happens to their outer shell electrons.
walkthrough:
Picture the sea model**
In LiAl, the Li and Al atoms release their outer electrons to become positive ions packed in a regular lattice. Those electrons are free to move throughout the whole structure, and the strong electrostatic attraction between the cations and the mobile electrons is metallic bonding.
Final answer: Lattice of positive ions / cations surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons.

hints: Think which white hydroxide is formed from Al species in water and dissolves in excess alkali to give an aluminate ion.
walkthrough:
Use the classic Al test**
$\text{LiAlH}_4$ hydrolyses to give $\text{Al}^{3+}$ which forms a white precipitate of $\text{Al}(\text{OH})_3$ with water. The clue that it dissolves in excess $\text{NaOH}$ confirms it, because aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric while most other white hydroxides are not.
Final answer: $\text{Al}(\text{OH})_3$ / aluminium hydroxide

hints: Look at reaction 1: a primary $-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ group becomes $-\text{COOH}$ while a secondary alcohol becomes a ketone. What strength of oxidant does full oxidation need?
Recall the standard oxidising mixture for primary alcohol to carboxylic acid and why heating under reflux rather than distillation is required here.
walkthrough:
Spot the level of oxidation**
Butane-1,2-diol to P converts $\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}$ to $\text{-COOH}$ and $\text{>CHOH}$ to $\text{>C=O}$. That is strong oxidation, so you need the powerful oxidant acidified potassium dichromate(VI).

Choose reflux to keep everything in**
You must heat under reflux with dilute acid. Reflux returns vapours to the flask so the intermediate aldehyde stays in contact with oxidant long enough to be oxidised fully to the acid, and the non volatile diol and keto acid are not lost.
Final answer: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI), $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7 / \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, heat under reflux.

hints: Compare the structures of P and the target 2-hydroxybutanoic acid to see which functional group must be reduced and which must be left alone.
Recall the key difference in reducing power: which hydride can reduce carboxylic acids and which stops at aldehydes and ketones.
walkthrough:
Map what must change**
P is $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{COCOOH}$. To get $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH(OH)COOH}$ you must reduce the ketone to a secondary alcohol but keep the carboxylic acid untouched. That needs a selective reagent.

Pick the gentle hydride**
$\text{NaBH}_4$ is the milder hydride source, it reduces aldehydes and ketones but leaves $\text{COOH}$ unchanged, so reaction 3 gives R correctly. $\text{LiAlH}_4$ is much stronger and would also reduce the acid to a primary alcohol, giving $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{OH}$ as Q, not the target.

Final answer: R is 2-hydroxybutanoic acid, only the ketone $\text{C=O}$ in P is reduced in reaction 3. $\text{NaBH}_4$ is a weaker reducing agent and cannot reduce $\text{COOH}$, whereas $\text{LiAlH}_4$ reduces both $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{COOH}$ so Q is the diol.

hints: Decide which species in $\text{NaCN/HCN}$ supplies the nucleophile and what feature of the aldehyde attracts it.
Think about how the $\text{C=O}$ bond is polarised and where the pair of electrons from the double bond must go when the new bond forms.
Consider what charge the oxygen carries after attack and what the full structure of that intermediate looks like.
Remember to show lone pairs, dipoles and the exact start and end points of each curly arrow.
walkthrough:
Name the attacker**
$\text{HCN}$ alone is a weak nucleophile, $\text{CN}^-$ from $\text{NaCN}$ is the real nucleophile. Draw it as $:C\equiv N:^ -$ with a lone pair on carbon, that lone pair will make the new bond.

Polarise the carbonyl**
Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so show $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ and $\text{O}^{\delta-}$ on $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CHO}$. The $\delta+$ carbon is the electrophile that attracts $\text{CN}^-$.

Push the first arrow**
Draw a curly arrow starting at the lone pair on $\text{CN}^-$ and pointing to the carbonyl carbon. At the same time draw a second curly arrow from the $\text{C=O}$ double bond up onto oxygen. This shows the pi bond breaking as the new $\text{C-C}$ bond forms.

Draw the alkoxide intermediate**
The product of attack is $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH(O}^-\text{)CN}$, with a negative charge and full lone pairs on oxygen and the $\text{CN}$ group now attached by a single bond to carbon. Later protonation by $\text{HCN}$ gives the cyanohydrin S.

Final answer: Nucleophile is $:\text{CN}^-$ with $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ triple bond shown. Curly arrow from $\text{CN}^-$ lone pair to carbonyl C of propanal ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CHO}$) with $\text{C}^{\delta+}\text{-O}^{\delta-}$ dipole shown, curly arrow from $\text{C=O}$ to O to give intermediate $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH(O}^-\text{)CN}$.

hints: Recall that heating a nitrile with aqueous acid adds two water molecules across $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ to give a carboxylic acid plus an ammonium salt.
walkthrough:
Hydrolyse the nitrile**
Heating S with $\text{HCl(aq)}$ hydrolyses $\text{-CN}$ to $\text{-COOH}$. Balance with $\text{HCl} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ on the left to give $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ alongside $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH(OH)COOH}$ on the right: $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH(OH)CN} + \text{HCl} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH(OH)COOH} + \text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$$

hints: List the key groups that differ between S (has $\text{OH}$ and $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$) and 2-hydroxybutanoic acid (has $\text{OH}$ and $\text{COOH}$) and recall their characteristic wavenumbers above $1500 \text{ cm}^{-1}$.
Look for a sharp absorption near $2200 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ and check for absence of acid $\text{C=O}$ near $1700 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ and broad acid $\text{O-H}$ near $2500-3000 \text{ cm}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Spot the nitrile fingerprint**
The spectrum shows a sharp dip at about $2200 \text{ cm}^{-1}$. That is the $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ stretch, which only S can show. The hydroxy acid has no triple bond, so this alone points strongly to S.

Confirm the acid is missing**
A carboxylic acid would show a strong $\text{C=O}$ absorption at $1680-1730 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ and a very broad $\text{O-H}$ band at $2500-3000 \text{ cm}^{-1}$. Both are absent here. The broad band near $3200-3600 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ is just the alcohol $\text{O-H}$ in S. Two pieces of evidence together identify S.

Final answer: Compound is S. Absorption at $2200-2250 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ due to $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ present in S but absent in acid. Lack of absorption at $1680-1730 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ ($\text{C=O}$ in acid) and / or lack of broad absorption at $2500-3000 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ ($\text{O-H}$ in $\text{RCOOH}$) shows acid absent. Any two valid points.
